reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: Historical-simulation 95% VaR, 260-day window, cut-off = the $(\alpha n + 1)$th worst return. Yesterday's worst 1-day returns (%) at ranks 12 to 15: $-6.40, -6.25, -6.05, -5.99$. Today the stock falls 10%, a new worst return, and a mild $-3\%$ return leaves the window (it was never in the tail).
ask: Today's cut-off return is closest to:

options.why: Shifted the cut-off two ranks down, as if a second extreme return had entered. Only one did.
Kept yesterday's cut-off. The new $-10\%$ becomes the worst return and pushes every tail return down one rank.
Moved the cut-off the wrong way, as if the leaving $-3\%$ return had been in the tail. It was not, so nothing moves up.

working.label: Effect of the new worst return
working.display: Yesterday's 13th worst ($-6.25\%$) is now the 14th worst

working.label: Today's cut-off
working.display: $-6.25\%$ (the leaving $-3\%$ changes nothing in the tail)

takeaway: A new extreme return enters the tail and shifts every rank down by one, so the cut-off becomes yesterday's one-rank-earlier return. A mild return leaving the window changes nothing.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: Stock A's last 260 daily returns are strongly negatively skewed: a long left tail (large losses) and a short right tail (large gains). Portfolio P1 is long a given amount of A and P2 is short the same amount. Both use 99% historical-simulation VaR.
ask: Which portfolio has the larger 99% VaR?

options.label: P2 (short)
options.why: Matched the short position to the long left tail. The short loses when A rises, so it is exposed to the short right tail.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: Assumed equal position size means equal VaR. HS reads the tail of the actual return distribution, and each side faces a different tail.

working.label: Long portfolio's loss tail
working.display: The long loses when returns fall, so its VaR sits in the long left tail

working.label: Short portfolio's loss tail
working.display: The short loses when returns rise, so its VaR sits in the short right tail

working.label: Compare
working.display: The left tail is the more extreme one, so the long portfolio has the larger VaR

takeaway: For HS VaR, read the tail on the side where the position loses. Negative skew punishes the long, not the short.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: 95% historical-simulation VaR, 260-day window, cut-off = 14th worst return $= -6.05\%$. Yesterday the position was worth USD 100, so VaR was USD 6.05. Today the stock rises 10%. Today's rally does not enter the left tail and the return leaving the window is not in the tail either.
ask: Today's USD VaR, compared with yesterday's USD 6.05, is:

options.label: The same
options.why: Kept the cut-off return $-6.05\%$ and the old USD 100 base. The percentage is unchanged, but it applies to today's larger position.

options.label: Lower
options.why: Took a rally to mean less risk. VaR is a loss percentage times the current position value, and the position just got bigger.

takeaway: In HS VaR the percentage cut-off comes from the return history, but the dollar figure is scaled by today's position value.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: An asset is worth USD 100 at the start of the year and USD 112 at the end, and pays a USD 1.00 interim dividend (treat it as received at year-end). The discount rate is 3.0%. The discounted P/L is $(P_1 + D)/(1+d) - P_0$.
ask: The discounted year-end proceeds $(112 + 1)/1.03$ are closest to:

options.label: USD 113.0
options.why: Left the proceeds undiscounted. The 3% rate must reduce a year-end amount.

options.label: USD 116.4
options.why: Compounded instead of discounting: $113 \times 1.03$. Discounting divides by $1+d$.

takeaway: Discount the year-end value plus the dividend first, then subtract the starting value. Proceeds land just under 110 and the profit just under 10.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: Expected shortfall can be written as a weighted average of loss quantiles, with weights that sum (integrate) to 1. For 95% ES, quantiles outside the worst 5% get zero weight and every quantile inside the 5% tail gets the same constant weight.
ask: That constant tail weight is closest to:

options.why: Used the tail probability itself as the weight. The tail would then carry only $0.05 \times 0.05 = 0.0025$ of the total weight.
Gave each tail quantile weight 1, as in a plain average. That carries only $0.05$ of total weight, not 1.
Read 5% as 5. The tail would then carry $0.05 \times 5 = 0.25$ of the total weight.

takeaway: ES weight is $1/(1-c)$ on each tail quantile, so the weights re-total to 1. A thin tail needs a large weight.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: Estimating 95% ES for a standard normal loss by slicing the 5% tail into five equal-probability slices gives four tail VaRs: 96%: 1.75, 97%: 1.88, 98%: 2.05, 99%: 2.33. The ES estimate is their simple average. The midpoint of the lowest and highest is $(1.75 + 2.33)/2 = 2.04$.
ask: Compared with that midpoint, the average of the four tail VaRs is:

options.label: Above 2.04
options.why: Expected a fatter tail to push the average above the midpoint. The tail VaRs are not evenly spaced: the gaps widen (0.13, 0.17, 0.28), so more of them sit near the low end.

options.label: Equal to 2.04
options.why: Assumed the four tail VaRs are evenly spaced, as in a straight line. Normal quantiles climb faster further out.

takeaway: Normal tail quantiles speed up as you go out, so their average sits below the midpoint of the lowest and highest. The estimate is about 2.00.

reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
setup: An equity portfolio holds $N = 3{,}000$ stocks, each treated as its own risk factor, so a full covariance matrix has $N^2 = 9{,}000{,}000$ cells. Each distinct pair of different factors needs one covariance term.
ask: The number of distinct covariance terms between different factors is about:

options.label: All of $N^2$ (about 9 million)
options.why: Counted both $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$, and the diagonal. A covariance between two factors is one number, and the diagonal holds variances.

options.label: About $N$ (3,000)
options.why: Counted one term per factor and left out the cross terms. Every pair of factors needs its own covariance.

takeaway: Distinct pairs number $N(N-1)/2$, about half of $N^2$. That explosion is why large books are mapped onto a few general factors.

reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
setup: Four stocks, 25% each, all mapped to the market. Portfolio beta $0.90$, market volatility 2.0% per day, each stock's idiosyncratic volatility 3.0% per day, uncorrelated with the market and with each other. $V(R_p) = \beta_p^2 V(R_m) + \sum w_i^2 \sigma_{\epsilon i}^2$.
ask: The specific (idiosyncratic) variance term $\sum w_i^2\sigma_{\epsilon i}^2$, in $(\%)^2$, is closest to:

options.why: Used only one stock: $0.25^2 \times 3^2 = 0.5625$. The sum runs over all four.
Dropped the weights and took one stock's $3^2$. With four 25% stakes the weights shrink the term to a quarter.

takeaway: Diversifying across four independent names cuts specific variance to a quarter of one stock's. The market term, $\beta^2\sigma_m^2$, is what remains.

reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
setup: An USD 80m equity book has four equal USD 20m positions with betas 0.50, 0.90, 1.10 and 1.30 to the market. Market volatility is 1.0% per day. Returns are zero-mean normal and specific risk is zero.
ask: The one-day 95% VaR ($z = 1.645$) is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.31m
options.why: Applied the average beta $0.95$ to one USD 20m position instead of to the whole book.

options.label: ≈ USD 5.0m
options.why: Multiplied the sum of betas (3.80) by the full USD 80m. Each beta only scales its own USD 20m.

options.label: ≈ USD 19.8m
options.why: Annualised the daily volatility with $\sqrt{252}$ even though the horizon is one day.

takeaway: Beta-weight each position's dollars first, add them up, then multiply by the market's $z\sigma$.

reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
setup: A two-bond book is cash-flow mapped to zero vertices, with perfectly correlated zero rates, so vertex VaRs add. Each zero's VaR is $PV \times z \times \sigma \times T/(1+y)$ with $z = 2.326$, yield volatility $\sigma = 1.0\%$. The 1-year vertex has PV USD 104.85m at $y = 3.0\%$. The 5-year vertex has PV USD 87.14m at $y = 3.8\%$.
ask: Which of these two vertices contributes the larger dollar VaR?

options.label: The 1-year vertex
options.why: Went by the larger PV (104.85 vs 87.14). The VaR rate grows with $T$, so the 5-year zero's rate is about five times the 1-year's.

options.label: About equal
options.why: Saw similar PVs and stopped. The $T/(1+y)$ factor differs by a factor of about 4.9 between the two vertices.

takeaway: A vertex's VaR is its PV times a rate that rises with maturity. A smaller PV far out the curve usually beats a bigger PV near the front.

reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
setup: USD 100m 7-year pay-fixed swap. Fixed-leg modified duration 5.90; the floating leg has just reset, with duration about 1.0. Flat curve, annual yield volatility 100 bp, normal approximation ($z = 2.326$ at 99%), square-root-of-time scaling.
ask: The one-month 99% VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.67m
options.why: Used only the floater's duration of 1.0. A pay-fixed swap is short the fixed leg and long the floater, so the net duration is $5.90 - 1.00$.

options.label: ≈ USD 11.4m
options.why: Used the full annual 100 bp volatility for a one-month horizon. It must be scaled by $\sqrt{1/12}$.

options.label: ≈ USD 39.5m
options.why: Scaled the volatility up by $\sqrt{12}$ instead of down.

takeaway: Swap duration is the fixed leg minus the floater. Scale annual yield volatility down by $\sqrt{12}$ for one month.

reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
setup: A fund holds 5,000 deep in-the-money calls, 20,000 deep out-of-the-money calls and 10,000 forwards on TUV (no dividends), one share each. TUV trades at USD 52 with volatility 12% per year. Use 252 trading days.
ask: The one-day 99% VaR ($z = 2.326$) is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 860
options.why: Divided the annual volatility by 252 instead of $\sqrt{252}$.

options.label: ≈ USD 4,600
options.why: Dropped the 10,000 forwards. A forward has delta 1, so they add as much exposure as the deep ITM calls and more.

options.label: ≈ USD 218,000
options.why: Used the 12% annual volatility for a one-day horizon.

takeaway: Deep ITM options and forwards count at delta 1, deep OTM options at about 0. Scale annual volatility by $\sqrt{252}$, not 252.

reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
setup: A company is long (buys) a 6-month FRA, notional USD 10m, contract rate 4.00%: it locks in a borrowing rate. At the start of the period the 6-month reference rate is 4.60% (simple, semiannual accrual). Settlement is paid at the start of the period, discounted at the reference rate.
ask: The buyer's settlement is:

options.label: Receives the full USD 30,000
options.why: Left the payment undiscounted. Settling at the start of the period instead of the end means dividing by $1 + 0.046 \times 0.5$.

options.label: Pays about USD 29,000
options.why: Flipped the sign. The reference rate (4.60%) is above the contract rate (4.00%), so the borrower who locked in 4.00% gains.

takeaway: The FRA buyer gains when the reference rate ends above the contract rate. Payment at the start of the period shrinks the end-of-period amount by the discount factor.

reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
setup: EUR spot is USD 1.3988 per EUR. The 1-year EUR interest rate is 2.28% and the 1-year USD rate is 3.33% (annual compounding).
ask: The one-year forward rate (USD per EUR) is:

options.label: Below 1.3988
options.why: Put the EUR rate in the numerator: $1.3988 \times 1.0228/1.0333 = 1.3846$. The currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount, and USD is the high-rate side here.

options.label: Equal to 1.3988
options.why: Ignored the rate gap. Forwards equal spot only when both rates are equal.

takeaway: Forward = spot $\times (1 + r_{\text{quote}})/(1 + r_{\text{base}})$. The base currency (EUR) is at a forward premium when the quote currency (USD) has the higher rate.

reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
setup: An asset has spot price 1.22. The domestic risk-free rate is 3.70% and the asset's income yield is 1.92%, both continuously compounded. The forward price is $F = S e^{(r-y)T}$ with $T = 1$ year.
ask: The carry exponent $(r - y)T$ is:

options.why: Added the yield to the rate. Income earned on the asset lowers the forward, so it is subtracted.
Flipped to $y - r$. The financing cost (3.70%) exceeds the income (1.92%), so net carry is positive.

takeaway: A forward costs financing minus income. Net carry is positive here, so the forward sits above spot.

reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
setup: Seven paired observations. A: 3, 4, 4, 6, 8, 9, 7. B: 5, 4, 7, 4, 2, 2, 1. Means: $E(A) = 5.857$, $E(B) = 3.571$. The mean of the products is $E(AB) = 17.714$.
ask: $\text{Cov}(A,B) = E(AB) - E(A)E(B)$ is closest to:

options.why: Subtracted the other way round: $E(A)E(B) - E(AB)$. Large A values pair with small B values, so the covariance is negative.
Used $E(AB)$ alone and forgot to subtract the product of the means.

takeaway: Covariance is the mean of the products minus the product of the means. When A is high and B is low it comes out negative (here $\rho \approx -0.80$).

reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
setup: A two-asset portfolio holds USD 7m of A (daily standard deviation 2%) and USD 5m of B (daily standard deviation 1%). The correlation is 0.4.
ask: The 10-day 99% VaR ($z = 2.33$) is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.12m
options.why: Divided by $\sqrt{10}$ instead of multiplying: the horizon grows risk.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.39m
options.why: Stopped at the one-day VaR and forgot the $\sqrt{10}$ scaling.

options.label: ≈ USD 3.9m
options.why: Scaled the one-day VaR by 10 instead of $\sqrt{10}$.

takeaway: Combine position volatilities with the correlation first, then scale by $z$ and by $\sqrt{\text{days}}$.

reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
setup: A portfolio has two positions whose stand-alone VaRs are USD 10m and USD 40m. Their returns are uncorrelated.
ask: The portfolio VaR lies:

options.label: Below 40m
options.why: Applied a diversification benefit to the larger VaR. Uncorrelated risks still add in quadrature, so the total exceeds its largest part.

options.label: At 50m
options.why: Added the two VaRs in a straight line, which assumes perfect correlation.

working.label: Bounds
working.display: Above $40$ (the largest part), below $50$ (the straight sum)

takeaway: Uncorrelated VaRs combine as $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$: always above the biggest part, below the straight sum.

reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
setup: Equally weighted two-asset portfolio of USD 20m, each asset with daily volatility 2%, correlation $\rho$. $\sigma_P = \sigma\sqrt{0.5(1+\rho)}$. The 10-day 99% VaR ($z = 2.33$) is USD 2.33m.
ask: The correlation $\rho$ implied by that VaR is:

options.why: This is the doubled correlation, the end of the chain. The question needs the starting value first.
Assumed uncorrelated assets. That would give a VaR of about USD 2.08m, not 2.33m.
Assumed perfect correlation. That would give a VaR of about USD 2.95m, not 2.33m.

takeaway: Strip the VaR back to a daily portfolio volatility and compare it with $\sigma\sqrt{0.5}$ ($\rho=0$) and $\sigma$ ($\rho=1$). Here $\rho$ sits at 0.25.

reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
setup: Two borrowers have default probabilities of 5% (A) and 10% (B). The binomial default correlation is $+0.6$.
ask: The joint default probability $P(A \cap B)$ lies:

options.label: Below 0.5%
options.why: Treated positive correlation as lowering the joint probability. Independence gives $5\% \times 10\% = 0.5\%$, and positive correlation lifts it above that.

options.label: Above 5%
options.why: Read $\rho = 0.6$ as a 60% joint probability. Joint default can never exceed the smaller marginal PD, 5%.

takeaway: Positive default correlation puts the joint PD above $P_A P_B$ and always under $\min(P_A, P_B)$.

reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
setup: Two loans: $PD(X) = 10.0\%$, $PD(Y) = 4.0\%$, joint default probability $PD(X \text{ and } Y) = 3.930\%$.
ask: The numerator of the binomial default correlation, $P(X \cap Y) - P_X P_Y$, is closest to:

options.why: Took the joint probability as the numerator. The benchmark $P_X P_Y$ must be taken out first.
Used the independence benchmark $P_X P_Y = 10\% \times 4\%$ alone and dropped the joint probability.

takeaway: Default correlation measures joint default above what independence would give. Take $P_X P_Y$ off first, then divide by the product of the standard deviations.

reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
setup: A trader buys USD 100m face of the 20-year Treasury and hedges by selling 10-year and 30-year bonds. A regression of 20-year yield changes on 10-year and 30-year changes gives $\beta_{10} = 0.53$ and $\beta_{30} = 0.74$. Each hedge leg is sized so that its DV01 equals its $\beta$ times the 20-year position's DV01.
ask: Total DV01 of the two hedge legs, compared with the 20-year position's DV01, is:

options.label: Smaller
options.why: Averaged the betas ($0.635$) instead of adding them. The two legs together hedge the same yield move, so their DV01s add.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Assumed a regression hedge is DV01-neutral. It minimises residual variance, not DV01 difference, and the betas need not sum to 1.

working.label: Hedge DV01 relative to the 20-year DV01

takeaway: In a two-factor regression hedge the DV01 ratio equals $\beta_{10} + \beta_{30}$. Nothing forces it to be 1.

reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
setup: A market maker is receiving fixed on USD 100m of a 20-year swap and hedges with 10-year and 30-year swaps. DV01 per 100 face: 10-year 0.030, 20-year 0.090, 30-year 0.150. Regression betas of 20-year rate changes: $\beta_{10} = 0.2221$ and $\beta_{30} = 0.7765$. Hedge face $F_i = F_{20} \times (DV01_{20}/DV01_i) \times \beta_i$.
ask: Which hedge leg needs the larger face amount?

options.label: The 30-year swap
options.why: Followed the larger beta (0.78 vs 0.22) and ignored the DV01 ratio. A 10-year swap has one fifth of a 30-year swap's DV01, so it needs far more face per unit of DV01.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: Assumed equal DV01 contributions mean equal face. Face amounts differ because each swap's DV01 per 100 differs.

takeaway: A bond with a small DV01 per 100 needs a big face to carry a given DV01. Beta alone does not set the face amount.
